claim: Macropinocytic cups in Dictyostelium are organised around coincident intense patches of PIP3, active Ras and active Rac.
source: We show that macropinocytic cups in Dictyostelium are organised around coincident intense patches of PIP3, active Ras and active Rac.
evidence: This is stated as a primary finding in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in figures throughout the manuscript.

claim: Signalling patches are invariably associated with a ring of active SCAR/WAVE at their periphery.
source: These signalling patches are invariably associated with a ring of active SCAR/WAVE at their periphery, as are all examined structures based on PIP3 patches, including phagocytic cups and basal waves.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative data in Figures 2, 3, and 5.

claim: Patch formation does not depend on the enclosing F-actin ring.
source: Patch formation does not depend on the enclosing F-actin ring, and patches become enlarged when the RasGAP NF1 is mutated, showing that Ras plays an instructive role.
evidence: This is supported by latrunculin-A experiments shown in Figure 7A-H demonstrating that PIP3 patches persist when actin is depolymerized.

claim: Patches become enlarged when the RasGAP NF1 is mutated.
source: Patch formation does not depend on the enclosing F-actin ring, and patches become enlarged when the RasGAP NF1 is mutated, showing that Ras plays an instructive role.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing NF1 knockout cells with parental cells in Figure 7K-L.

claim: Ras plays an instructive role in macropinocytic cup formation.
source: Patch formation does not depend on the enclosing F-actin ring, and patches become enlarged when the RasGAP NF1 is mutated, showing that Ras plays an instructive role.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that manipulating Ras activity through NF1 mutation directly affects patch size.

claim: New macropinocytic cups predominantly form by splitting from existing ones.
source: New macropinocytic cups predominantly form by splitting from existing ones.
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 1E showing 62% of macropinocytic cups (94 out of 152) originate by splitting.

claim: 62% of macropinocytic cups initiate by splitting of existing ones (n = 152).
source: 3D movies show that the majority of macropinocytic cups initiate by splitting of existing ones (62%; n = 152, Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from lattice light sheet microscopy data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Macropinocytosis is a fundamental mechanism that allows cells to take up extracellular liquid into large vesicles.
source: Macropinocytosis is a fundamental mechanism that allows cells to take up extracellular liquid into large vesicles.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology supported by multiple citations in the introduction.

claim: Macropinocytosis critically depends on the formation of a ring of protrusive actin beneath the plasma membrane.
source: It critically depends on the formation of a ring of protrusive actin beneath the plasma membrane, which develops into the macropinocytic cup.
evidence: This is supported by the F-actin imaging data throughout the manuscript and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Macropinocytosis is used for feeding by amoebae.
source: It is an ancient process, used for feeding by amoebae (Hacker et al., 1997; Thilo and Vogel, 1980), but one that is important for a wide spectrum of human biology, including uptake of drugs, and large-scale sampling of extracellular medium for antigens by immune cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hacker et al., 1997 and Thilo and Vogel, 1980.

claim: Macropinocytosis is important for uptake of drugs in human biology.
source: It is an ancient process, used for feeding by amoebae (Hacker et al., 1997; Thilo and Vogel, 1980), but one that is important for a wide spectrum of human biology, including uptake of drugs, and large-scale sampling of extracellular medium for antigens by immune cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about macropinocytosis function.

claim: Macropinocytosis is important for large-scale sampling of extracellular medium for antigens by immune cells.
source: It is an ancient process, used for feeding by amoebae (Hacker et al., 1997; Thilo and Vogel, 1980), but one that is important for a wide spectrum of human biology, including uptake of drugs, and large-scale sampling of extracellular medium for antigens by immune cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about macropinocytosis function in immune cells.

claim: Macropinocytosis has been hijacked by pathogens as a major route of entry.
source: It has also been hijacked by pathogens as a major route of entry (Mercer and Helenius, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mercer and Helenius, 2012.

claim: Macropinocytosis is a principal and widely used method for sustaining the excessive metabolic demands of cancer cells.
source: Recent data suggest that macropinocytosis is a principal and widely used method for sustaining the excessive metabolic demands of cancer cells (Commisso et al., 2013; Kamphorst et al., 2015) and may be implicated in the spread of neurodegenerative disease within the brain (Münch et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Commisso et al., 2013 and Kamphorst et al., 2015.

claim: Macropinocytosis may be implicated in the spread of neurodegenerative disease within the brain.
source: Recent data suggest that macropinocytosis is a principal and widely used method for sustaining the excessive metabolic demands of cancer cells (Commisso et al., 2013; Kamphorst et al., 2015) and may be implicated in the spread of neurodegenerative disease within the brain (Münch et al., 2011).
evidence: This is presented as a speculative possibility supported by citation to Münch et al., 2011.

claim: Macropinosomes form from cup-shaped extensions of the plasma membrane, often known as circular ruffles.
source: Macropinosomes form from cup-shaped extensions of the plasma membrane, often known as circular ruffles, which are extended by actin polymerisation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about macropinosome formation.

claim: Circular ruffles are extended by actin polymerisation.
source: Macropinosomes form from cup-shaped extensions of the plasma membrane, often known as circular ruffles, which are extended by actin polymerisation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of circular ruffle extension.

claim: The leading rims of circular ruffles must be driven outwards to enclose liquid.
source: The leading rims of these ruffles must be driven outwards to enclose liquid – often for a very significant fraction of the cell's diameter – but the base must be held static.
evidence: This is a logical description of the mechanical requirements for macropinocytic cup formation.

claim: The base of circular ruffles must be held static during macropinocytic cup formation.
source: The leading rims of these ruffles must be driven outwards to enclose liquid – often for a very significant fraction of the cell's diameter – but the base must be held static.
evidence: This is a logical description of the mechanical requirements for macropinocytic cup formation.

claim: Macropinocytic cups can be several microns in diameter.
source: The resulting cups can be several microns in diameter, and eventually close by constriction of their rim, with membrane fusion producing an endocytic vesicle.
evidence: This is supported by the scale bars and measurements shown in the figures throughout the manuscript.

claim: Macropinocytic cups eventually close by constriction of their rim, with membrane fusion producing an endocytic vesicle.
source: The resulting cups can be several microns in diameter, and eventually close by constriction of their rim, with membrane fusion producing an endocytic vesicle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about macropinocytic cup closure and is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In phagocytosis, cup formation is guided by engaging receptors with the particle to be engulfed in a zippering process.
source: In the closely related process of phagocytosis, in which solid particles are taken up, it is proposed that cup formation is guided by engaging receptors with the particle to be engulfed in a zippering process (Freeman and Grinstein, 2014; Griffin et al., 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Freeman and Grinstein, 2014 and Griffin et al., 1975.

claim: Macropinosomes take up fluid and cannot use a particle as a template.
source: However, macropinosomes take up fluid and so cannot use a particle as a template in this way.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the fundamental difference between phagocytosis and macropinocytosis.

claim: There is no known equivalent in macropinocytosis of the coat that organises clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: Nor is there any known equivalent in macropinocytosis of the coat that organises clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge about macropinocytosis mechanisms.

claim: Macropinocytic cups must form by a self-organizing process within the actin polymerization machinery and its regulators.
source: Thus it appears that macropinocytic cups must form by a self-organizing process within the actin polymerization machinery and its regulators.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of external templates or organizing coats.

claim: ForG is needed for the basal part of phagocytic cups in Dictyostelium.
source: The dynamic actin that polymerises around macropinocytic cups is probably initiated by a number of nucleators, including both formins, such as ForG, which is needed for the basal part of phagocytic cups in Dictyostelium (Junemann et al., 2016), and the Arp2/3 complex (Insall et al., 2001), which produces dendritic structures (Pollard and Borisy, 2003), like the actin that drives pseudopods.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Junemann et al., 2016.

claim: The Arp2/3 complex produces dendritic actin structures.
source: The dynamic actin that polymerises around macropinocytic cups is probably initiated by a number of nucleators, including both formins, such as ForG, which is needed for the basal part of phagocytic cups in Dictyostelium (Junemann et al., 2016), and the Arp2/3 complex (Insall et al., 2001), which produces dendritic structures (Pollard and Borisy, 2003), like the actin that drives pseudopods.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Insall et al., 2001 and Pollard and Borisy, 2003.

claim: Assembly of Arp2/3 based actin is controlled by the WASP family of nucleation promoting factors.
source: Assembly of Arp2/3 based actin is controlled by the WASP family of nucleation promoting factors; the two family members that act at the plasma membrane are WASP and SCAR/WAVE (hereafter called SCAR).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Arp2/3 regulation.

claim: WASP and SCAR/WAVE are the two WASP family members that act at the plasma membrane.
source: Assembly of Arp2/3 based actin is controlled by the WASP family of nucleation promoting factors; the two family members that act at the plasma membrane are WASP and SCAR/WAVE (hereafter called SCAR).
evidence: This is established knowledge about WASP family localization.

claim: WASP is important for actin polymerisation during clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: WASP is important for actin polymerisation during clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Taylor et al., 2011), and SCAR, acting in a five-membered complex (Eden et al., 2002), for the formation of pseudopods (Seastone et al., 2001; Veltman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2011.

claim: SCAR acts in a five-membered complex.
source: WASP is important for actin polymerisation during clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Taylor et al., 2011), and SCAR, acting in a five-membered complex (Eden et al., 2002), for the formation of pseudopods (Seastone et al., 2001; Veltman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eden et al., 2002.

claim: SCAR is important for the formation of pseudopods.
source: WASP is important for actin polymerisation during clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Taylor et al., 2011), and SCAR, acting in a five-membered complex (Eden et al., 2002), for the formation of pseudopods (Seastone et al., 2001; Veltman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Seastone et al., 2001 and Veltman et al., 2012.

claim: Ras and phosphoinositide signalling help organize the cytoskeleton for macropinocytosis and phagocytosis.
source: Ras and phosphoinositide signalling help organize the cytoskeleton for macropinocytosis and phagocytosis (Bar-Sagi and Feramisco, 1986; Bloomfield and Kay, 2016; Bohdanowicz and Grinstein, 2013; Rodriguez-Viciana et al., 1997; Swanson, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Bar-Sagi and Feramisco, 1986; Bloomfield and Kay, 2016; Bohdanowicz and Grinstein, 2013; Rodriguez-Viciana et al., 1997; Swanson, 2014.

claim: Ras activity stimulates macropinocytosis in both mammalian and Dictyostelium cells.
source: There is evidence that Ras activity stimulates macropinocytosis in both mammalian and Dictyostelium cells, and macropinocytic cups are associated with an intense domain, or 'patch', of PIP3 (Araki et al., 2007; Parent et al., 1998; Yoshida et al., 2009), which is essential for their function (Araki et al., 1996; Buczynski et al., 1997; Hoeller et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Araki et al., 2007; Parent et al., 1998; Yoshida et al., 2009.

claim: Macropinocytic cups are associated with an intense domain, or 'patch', of PIP3.
source: There is evidence that Ras activity stimulates macropinocytosis in both mammalian and Dictyostelium cells, and macropinocytic cups are associated with an intense domain, or 'patch', of PIP3 (Araki et al., 2007; Parent et al., 1998; Yoshida et al., 2009), which is essential for their function (Araki et al., 1996; Buczynski et al., 1997; Hoeller et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations and confirmed by the experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: PIP3 patches are essential for macropinocytic cup function.
source: There is evidence that Ras activity stimulates macropinocytosis in both mammalian and Dictyostelium cells, and macropinocytic cups are associated with an intense domain, or 'patch', of PIP3 (Araki et al., 2007; Parent et al., 1998; Yoshida et al., 2009), which is essential for their function (Araki et al., 1996; Buczynski et al., 1997; Hoeller et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Araki et al., 1996; Buczynski et al., 1997; Hoeller et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 1998.

claim: In macrophages, ruffle circularisation creates a diffusion barrier in the membrane leading to intensified PIP3 signalling.
source: In macrophages, which often evolve macropinocytic cups from linear ruffles, it has been suggested that ruffle circularisation creates a diffusion barrier in the membrane leading to intensified PIP3 signalling and a domain of PIP3 in the centre of the circular ruffle (Welliver et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Welliver et al., 2011.

claim: The PIP3 domain in circular ruffles drives the further progression of the macropinocytic cup.
source: In macrophages, which often evolve macropinocytic cups from linear ruffles, it has been suggested that ruffle circularisation creates a diffusion barrier in the membrane leading to intensified PIP3 signalling and a domain of PIP3 in the centre of the circular ruffle (Welliver et al., 2011). This domain then drives the further progression of the macropinocytic cup.
evidence: This is inferred from the model proposed by Welliver et al., 2011.

claim: Macropinocytosis is massively up-regulated in axenic strains of Dictyostelium due to mutation of the RasGAP neurofibromatosis-1 (NF1).
source: In axenic strains of Dictyostelium, which grow efficiently in liquid medium, macropinocytosis is massively up-regulated due to mutation of the RasGAP neurofibromatosis-1 (NF1) (Bloomfield et al., 2015; Hacker et al., 1997; Kayman and Clarke, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bloomfield et al., 2015; Hacker et al., 1997; Kayman and Clarke, 1983.

claim: Axenic strains of Dictyostelium grow efficiently in liquid medium.
source: In axenic strains of Dictyostelium, which grow efficiently in liquid medium, macropinocytosis is massively up-regulated due to mutation of the RasGAP neurofibromatosis-1 (NF1) (Bloomfield et al., 2015; Hacker et al., 1997; Kayman and Clarke, 1983).
evidence: This is established knowledge about axenic Dictyostelium strains.

claim: Splitting occurs by simple division in the middle of macropinocytic cups.
source: Splitting occurs by a variety of routes, including: simple division in the middle; detachment of a small ruffle that grows into a new macropinocytic cup (Figure 1A, Video 1); and abortive fragmentation of a parental macropinocytic cup into multiple daughter cups.
evidence: This is observed in the lattice light sheet microscopy data shown in Figure 1 and Videos.

claim: Splitting occurs by detachment of a small ruffle that grows into a new macropinocytic cup.
source: Splitting occurs by a variety of routes, including: simple division in the middle; detachment of a small ruffle that grows into a new macropinocytic cup (Figure 1A, Video 1); and abortive fragmentation of a parental macropinocytic cup into multiple daughter cups.
evidence: This is observed in the lattice light sheet microscopy data shown in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: Splitting occurs by abortive fragmentation of a parental macropinocytic cup into multiple daughter cups.
source: Splitting occurs by a variety of routes, including: simple division in the middle; detachment of a small ruffle that grows into a new macropinocytic cup (Figure 1A, Video 1); and abortive fragmentation of a parental macropinocytic cup into multiple daughter cups.
evidence: This is observed in the lattice light sheet microscopy data.

claim: Active Rac is spatiotemporally associated tightly with F-actin during macropinocytic cup splitting.
source: We examined a reporter for active Rac in some of these movies and found that it is spatiotemporally associated tightly with F-actin in this morphological process (Figure 1B, Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dual-color imaging shown in Figure 1B and Video 2.

claim: De novo macropinocytic cups form in more than 90% of cases close to the base of the cell.
source: The remaining macropinocytic cups form de novo, expanding from places where no previous F-actin activity was detected. In more than 90% of cases the initiation is close to the base of the cell, even though most mature macropinocytic cups are present on the top, and are commonly described as 'crowns'.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the lattice light sheet microscopy data.

claim: Most mature macropinocytic cups are present on the top of the cell.
source: The remaining macropinocytic cups form de novo, expanding from places where no previous F-actin activity was detected. In more than 90% of cases the initiation is close to the base of the cell, even though most mature macropinocytic cups are present on the top, and are commonly described as 'crowns'.
evidence: This is observed in the lattice light sheet microscopy data.

claim: Circular ruffles can persist on the cell surface for prolonged periods before either closing successfully or regressing back into the cell body.
source: Circular ruffles can persist on the cell surface for prolonged periods before either closing successfully or regressing back into the cell body.
evidence: This is observed in time-lapse imaging data.

claim: Closure of the macropinocytic cup can be quite abrupt and often appears to involve the inward collapse of the rim.
source: Closure of the cup can be quite abrupt and often appears to involve the inward collapse of the rim (Figure 1F, Video 5) (Swanson et al., 1999).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 1F and Video 5, and is consistent with Swanson et al., 1999.

claim: Pseudopods are distinguished from macropinocytic circular ruffles by their shape, which is convex instead of concave.
source: The other large F-actin projections in growing Dictyostelium cells are pseudopods. These are distinguished from macropinocytic circular ruffles by their shape, which is convex instead of concave.
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the imaging data.

claim: De novo pseudopods initiate close to the substratum.
source: De novo pseudopods also initiate close to the substratum (Figure 1G, white arrow and Video 6) and expand steadily to their full size.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 1G and Video 6.

claim: Pseudopods are rare in growing axenic cells, accounting for less than 5% of all large F-actin structures.
source: Pseudopods are surprisingly rare in growing axenic cells, accounting for less than 5% of all large F-actin structures.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the lattice light sheet microscopy data.

claim: Actin waves move across the basal surface of vegetative cells.
source: Finally, we could follow the enigmatic actin waves that move across the basal surface of vegetative cells (Bretschneider et al., 2004, 2009; Gerisch, 2010).
evidence: This is observed in the imaging data and supported by citations to Bretschneider et al., 2004, 2009 and Gerisch, 2010.

claim: Basal waves generally originate from existing ruffles by splitting.
source: These waves also generally originate from existing ruffles by splitting.
evidence: This is observed in the lattice light sheet microscopy data.

claim: The large macropinocytic cups of axenic Dictyostelium cells generally form by splitting or by expanding de novo from a small focus.
source: These observations show that the large macropinocytic cups of axenic Dictyostelium cells generally form by splitting or by expanding de novo from a small focus, as in fibroblasts (Bernitt et al., 2015), rather than by circularization of linear ruffles (Welliver and Swanson, 2012).
evidence: This is concluded from the quantitative analysis in Figure 1E and supported by comparison to Bernitt et al., 2015.

claim: The smaller macropinocytic cups of wild-type cells more normally form de novo or by splitting, rather than by circularization.
source: The smaller macropinocytic cups of wild-type cells (see later) also more normally form de novo or by splitting, rather than by circularization.
evidence: This is observed in the wild-type cell imaging data shown later in the manuscript.

claim: Either increased or decreased PIP3 levels are deleterious to fluid uptake and growth in liquid medium.
source: Either increased or decreased PIP3 levels (PTEN and PI3-kinase mutants) are deleterious to fluid uptake and growth in liquid medium, as expected from earlier work (Clark et al., 2014; Hoeller and Kay, 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mutant analysis in Table 1 and supported by citations to Clark et al., 2014 and Hoeller and Kay, 2007.

claim: Two independent RasG- mutants are substantially impaired in growth in liquid medium.
source: Two independent RasG- mutants are substantially impaired in growth in liquid medium, as previously described, but contrary to the earlier report (Khosla et al., 2000), both are also defective in fluid uptake.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with mean generation times of 27.6 and 19.1 hours compared to 9.26 hours for Ax2.

claim: RasG- mutants are defective in fluid uptake.
source: Two independent RasG- mutants are substantially impaired in growth in liquid medium, as previously described, but contrary to the earlier report (Khosla et al., 2000), both are also defective in fluid uptake.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with fluid uptake values of 55.3 and 67.6 nl/10^6 cells/h compared to 114.7 for Ax2.

claim: RasC null cells have no growth defect.
source: RasC null cells have no growth defect and a lesser defect in fluid uptake, while RasS (not tested here) may also contribute to macropinocytosis (Chubb et al., 2000).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with a mean generation time of 9.27 hours, essentially identical to Ax2.

claim: RasC null cells have a lesser defect in fluid uptake.
source: RasC null cells have no growth defect and a lesser defect in fluid uptake, while RasS (not tested here) may also contribute to macropinocytosis (Chubb et al., 2000).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with fluid uptake of 84.3 nl/10^6 cells/h compared to 114.7 for Ax2.

claim: RasS may contribute to macropinocytosis.
source: RasC null cells have no growth defect and a lesser defect in fluid uptake, while RasS (not tested here) may also contribute to macropinocytosis (Chubb et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chubb et al., 2000.

claim: SCAR is required for efficient fluid uptake.
source: Notably, we confirm that the Arp2/3 activator, SCAR, is required for efficient fluid uptake (Seastone et al., 2001).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with two independent SCAR mutants showing reduced fluid uptake (56.8 and 19.7 nl/10^6 cells/h) compared to Ax2 (114.7), and is supported by citation to Seastone et al., 2001.

claim: The SCAR complex is mostly cytosolic and basally inactive.
source: The SCAR complex is mostly cytosolic and basally inactive, but when recruited to the plasma membrane it causes actin polymerization through the Arp2/3 complex (Steffen et al., 2004; Ura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Steffen et al., 2004 and Ura et al., 2012.

claim: When recruited to the plasma membrane, SCAR causes actin polymerization through the Arp2/3 complex.
source: The SCAR complex is mostly cytosolic and basally inactive, but when recruited to the plasma membrane it causes actin polymerization through the Arp2/3 complex (Steffen et al., 2004; Ura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Steffen et al., 2004 and Ura et al., 2012.

claim: A GFP reporter tagged at the HSPC300 subunit accumulates at sites of actin polymerization.
source: A GFP reporter tagged at the HSPC300 subunit accumulates at sites of actin polymerization (Veltman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Veltman et al., 2012 and confirmed by the data in Figure 2.

claim: The HSPC300-GFP reporter is recruited during pseudopod expansion phases but lost in stalls.
source: The results clearly show that the reporter is recruited during expansion phases but lost in stalls (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the kymograph analysis in Figure 2A-B.

claim: SCAR reporter intensity along the membrane correlates well with the local membrane expansion speed.
source: This correlation holds true globally: SCAR reporter intensity along the membrane correlates well with the local membrane expansion speed (Figure 2C) as all pixels with high SCAR reporter are associated with positive instantaneous membrane speed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the 2D histogram in Figure 2C showing correlation coefficient r = 0.56 (Pearson's).

claim: Pixels with very high membrane speeds and no SCAR are due to blebs.
source: Note that the small set of pixels with very high membrane speeds and no SCAR (Figure 2C, red arrow) are due to blebs (Zatulovskiy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the data pattern in Figure 2C and supported by citation to Zatulovskiy et al., 2014.

claim: SCAR is recruited as a ring to the lip of macropinocytic cups.
source: In images recorded in 3D, the reporter reveals a thin, sometimes broken ring of active SCAR around the lip of macropinocytic cups (Figure 2D and Video 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 3D reconstructions in Figure 2D and Video 8.

claim: The presence of a SCAR ring could not be predicted by imaging the actin cytoskeleton itself, as actin filaments are distributed rather uniformly throughout the cup.
source: The presence of a ring could not be predicted by imaging the actin cytoskeleton itself, as actin filaments are distributed rather uniformly throughout the cup (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing F-actin and SCAR distributions in Figure 2H.

claim: Circular SCAR structures are not seen in pseudopods.
source: These circular SCAR structures are not seen in pseudopods, where 3D images show the same discrete blocks of SCAR as in 2D images (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the 3D reconstruction of a pseudopod in Figure 2E.

claim: SCAR rings follow the edges of intensely stained domains, or 'patches' of PIP3.
source: We visualised PIP3 using a double reporter that co-expresses the PH-domain of CRAC fused to RFP (Insall et al., 1994). This revealed a second remarkable feature of SCAR rings: they follow the edges of intensely stained domains, or 'patches' (Postma et al., 2004) of PIP3.
evidence: This is demonstrated by dual-color imaging in Figures 2F-G and Video 9.

claim: In all macropinocytic cups examined, the concave cup contains a patch of PIP3 and SCAR is present as a ring around this patch, without detectable recruitment to its centre.
source: In all macropinocytic cups examined, of whatever size, the concave cup contains a patch of PIP3 and SCAR is present as a ring around this patch, without detectable recruitment to its centre (Figure 2F and G and Video 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 3D imaging in Figures 2F-G and Video 9, and quantified in Figure 3.

claim: All cup centres contained high levels of PIP3 (n=17 macropinocytic cups from nine cells).
source: This was confirmed in a larger sample by measuring fluorescence intensity at the centre and rim of 17 macropinocytic cups from nine cells rendered in 3D (Figure 3A–B). All cup centres contained high levels of PIP3, but SCAR consistently followed the rim of the cup with the mean fluorescence of the SCAR reporter significantly higher than cytosolic background (p<0.01), while signal at the centre of the PIP3 patch was not statistically different from the cytosolic background.
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 3A-B from 3D rendered images.

claim: The mean fluorescence of the SCAR reporter at the rim of macropinocytic cups is significantly higher than cytosolic background (p<0.01).
source: This was confirmed in a larger sample by measuring fluorescence intensity at the centre and rim of 17 macropinocytic cups from nine cells rendered in 3D (Figure 3A–B). All cup centres contained high levels of PIP3, but SCAR consistently followed the rim of the cup with the mean fluorescence of the SCAR reporter significantly higher than cytosolic background (p<0.01), while signal at the centre of the PIP3 patch was not statistically different from the cytosolic background.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the quantitative data in Figure 3B.

claim: SCAR signal at the centre of the PIP3 patch was not statistically different from the cytosolic background.
source: This was confirmed in a larger sample by measuring fluorescence intensity at the centre and rim of 17 macropinocytic cups from nine cells rendered in 3D (Figure 3A–B). All cup centres contained high levels of PIP3, but SCAR consistently followed the rim of the cup with the mean fluorescence of the SCAR reporter significantly higher than cytosolic background (p<0.01), while signal at the centre of the PIP3 patch was not statistically different from the cytosolic background.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the quantitative data in Figure 3B.

claim: SCAR is consistently and significantly enriched at PIP3 patch edges (p<0.01) in all cases examined.
source: In the first, a number of growing axenic cells was analysed as follows. Membrane areas with fluorescence intensity of the PIP3 reporter greater than cytosolic background plus one standard deviation were defined as PIP3 patches, and the associated SCAR signal was measured. In all cases SCAR is consistently and significantly enriched at patch edges (p<0.01), and never at their centres (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of 31 PIP3 patches shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: SCAR is never enriched at PIP3 patch centres.
source: In the first, a number of growing axenic cells was analysed as follows. Membrane areas with fluorescence intensity of the PIP3 reporter greater than cytosolic background plus one standard deviation were defined as PIP3 patches, and the associated SCAR signal was measured. In all cases SCAR is consistently and significantly enriched at patch edges (p<0.01), and never at their centres (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantitative analysis in Figure 3C-D.

claim: In pixels with high PIP3 signal, the SCAR signal is low, and conversely in pixels with high SCAR, PIP3 is low.
source: In the second test, the fluorescence intensity of the SCAR and PIP3 reporters was extracted from the circumference of a number of growing cells and the results plotted as a 2D histogram (Figure 3E). In pixels with high PIP3 signal, the SCAR signal is low, and conversely in pixels with high SCAR, PIP3 is low.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the 2D histogram in Figure 3E showing anti-correlation between SCAR and PIP3.

claim: SCAR and PIP3 do not co-localise but instead are anti-correlated.
source: This method cannot show whether high SCAR and PIP3 pixels are adjacent, but it does confirm that SCAR and PIP3 do not co-localise but instead are anti-correlated.
evidence: This is inferred from the 2D histogram analysis in Figure 3E.

claim: The PIP3 patch first becomes visible at t = 1 and this sub-micron sized patch is already flanked by puncta of SCAR.
source: The complete lifetime of a de novo macropinocytic cup is shown in Figure 4A (Video 10 shows another example). The PIP3 patch first becomes visible at t = 1 and this sub-micron sized patch is already flanked by puncta of SCAR.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging in Figure 4A.

claim: As the PIP3 patch grows the SCAR puncta remain dynamically associated with its edge right up to closure of the macropinocytic cup.
source: As the patch of PIP3 grows the SCAR puncta remain dynamically associated with its edge right up to closure of the macropinocytic cup, after which the SCAR signal quickly disappears and the vesicle is internalised.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging in Figure 4A and the kymograph in Figure 4B.

claim: After macropinocytic cup closure, the SCAR signal quickly disappears and the vesicle is internalised.
source: As the patch of PIP3 grows the SCAR puncta remain dynamically associated with its edge right up to closure of the macropinocytic cup, after which the SCAR signal quickly disappears and the vesicle is internalised.
evidence: This is observed in the time-lapse imaging data in Figure 4.

claim: SCAR is not detected at the centres of PIP3 patches above background.
source: The SCAR is not detected at the centres of the patches above background.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantitative analysis in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The SCAR signal can be traced along the edge of the PIP3 patches from the start of a patch to its abrupt loss at invagination.
source: This is also shown in a kymograph of the membrane pixels of a single cell as it makes several macropinosomes (Figure 4B). The SCAR signal, though sometimes weak, can be traced along the edge of the PIP3 patches from the start of a patch to its abrupt loss at invagination.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the kymograph in Figure 4B.

claim: SCAR remains associated with PIP3 patch edges throughout the macropinocytic cup lifetime despite changes in size and shape of PIP3 patches.
source: Combining the data from several macropinocytosis events confirms this continuous association (Figure 4C–E). Thus despite changes in size and shape of PIP3 patches, SCAR remains associated with their edges, and only their edges, throughout the macropinocytic cup lifetime.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantitative analysis of multiple macropinocytosis events in Figure 4C-E.

claim: During phagocytosis Dictyostelium cells make a PIP3 patch where they contact the particle to be ingested.
source: During phagocytosis Dictyostelium cells make a PIP3 patch where they contact the particle to be ingested (Clarke et al., 2010; Marshall et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clarke et al., 2010 and Marshall et al., 2001.

claim: During phagocytosis, SCAR is recruited to the edges of the PIP3 patch, and not the centre.
source: In the yeast case shown in Figure 5A, SCAR is recruited to the edges of the PIP3 patch, and not the centre, while a 3D view reveals a full ring of SCAR around the rim of the phagocytic cup.
evidence: This is demonstrated by 3D imaging of phagocytosis in Figure 5A.

claim: A clear ring of SCAR could be detected in all phagocytic cups examined, provided expression of the SCAR reporter was low enough to avoid excessive background fluorescence.
source: Indeed, a clear ring of SCAR could be detected in all such cases, provided expression of the SCAR reporter was low enough to avoid excessive background fluorescence.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation from the phagocytosis experiments.

claim: Basal waves have a core of PIP3 surrounded by a ring of F-actin.
source: Basal waves have a core of PIP3 surrounded by a ring of F-actin (Bretschneider et al., 2004, 2009; Gerhardt et al., 2014; Gerisch, 2010), and again, the basal PIP3 patches are invariably surrounded by a ring of SCAR (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bretschneider et al., 2004, 2009; Gerhardt et al., 2014; Gerisch, 2010.

claim: Basal PIP3 patches are invariably surrounded by a ring of SCAR.
source: Basal waves have a core of PIP3 surrounded by a ring of F-actin (Bretschneider et al., 2004, 2009; Gerhardt et al., 2014; Gerisch, 2010), and again, the basal PIP3 patches are invariably surrounded by a ring of SCAR (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy in Figure 5B.

claim: WASP is excluded from PIP3 patches and forms a ring around them, though weaker and less coherently than SCAR.
source: Basal waves are favourable for microscopy, and we found that WASP is also excluded from PIP3 patches and forms a ring around them, though weaker and less coherently than SCAR (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy of basal waves in Figure 5C.

claim: WASP forms rings at the edges of PIP3 patches of normal macropinocytic cups, more weakly than SCAR.
source: Similarly, WASP forms rings at the edges of PIP3 patches of normal macropinocytic cups, again more weakly than SCAR (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 3D imaging in Figure 5D.

claim: WASH does not associate with PIP3 patches.
source: The remaining Arp2/3 activator in Dictyostelium, WASH, does not associate with PIP3 patches (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: During chemotactic aggregation, streaming cells make head-to-tail attachments and form a domain of PIP3 in their anterior attachment.
source: During chemotactic aggregation, streaming cells make head-to-tail attachments and form a domain of PIP3 in their anterior attachment, which is surrounded by a strong SCAR ring; (F) A close-up of the region indicated in the white box in (E); (G) A full 3D reconstruction of the same contact site.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging in Figure 5E-G.

claim: PIP3 patches at cell-cell contacts are surrounded by a strong SCAR ring.
source: During chemotactic aggregation, streaming cells make head-to-tail attachments and form a domain of PIP3 in their anterior attachment, which is surrounded by a strong SCAR ring; (F) A close-up of the region indicated in the white box in (E); (G) A full 3D reconstruction of the same contact site.
evidence: This is demonstrated by 3D imaging in Figure 5E-G.

claim: Cells respond to cyclic-AMP by making PIP3, initially homogenously and then, after about a minute, in patches at the membrane.
source: Cells respond to cyclic-AMP by making PIP3, initially homogenously and then, after about a minute, in patches at the membrane (Postma et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Postma et al., 2004 and demonstrated in Figure 5H-J.

claim: SCAR is clearly at the edges of the PIP3 patches formed in response to cyclic-AMP stimulation.
source: In the low light conditions required for time-lapse imaging, the SCAR signal is weak, but where detected, it is clearly at the edges of the PIP3 patches (Figure 5H–J and Video 11).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging in Figure 5H-J and Video 11.

claim: Many PIP3 patches formed after cyclic-AMP stimulation become concave and close to engulf a drop of medium, indicating that the cell is performing macropinocytosis.
source: These patches have sometimes been regarded as new pseudopods (for example [Chen et al., 2003]), but many become concave and close to engulf a drop of medium, indicating that the cell is performing macropinocytosis, not a chemotactic response.
evidence: This is observed in the time-lapse imaging data.

claim: A patch of activated Ras exactly coincides with each PIP3 patch.
source: PIP3 is largely made by Ras-activated PI3-kinases (Clark et al., 2014; Funamoto et al., 2002; Hoeller and Kay, 2007). We confirmed that a patch of activated Ras exactly coincides with each PIP3 patch (Figure 6A) (Sasaki et al., 2004; 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dual-color imaging in Figure 6A and supported by citations.

claim: Plots of intensity, pixel-by-pixel, show exceptional correlation between the Ras and PIP3 signals.
source: Similarly, plots of intensity, pixel-by-pixel, show exceptional correlation between the Ras and PIP3 signals (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the 2D histogram in Figure 6B showing r = 0.85 (Pearson's) for n = 35 cells.

claim: PIP3 patches have a matching patch of activated Ras, which could sustain them by activating PI3-kinase.
source: Thus PIP3 patches have a matching patch of activated Ras, which could sustain them by activating PI3-kinase.
evidence: This is inferred from the coincidence of Ras and PIP3 patches and the known role of Ras in activating PI3-kinase.

claim: The Ras/PIP3 patch overlaps a patch of active Rac1.
source: Similarly, the Ras/PIP3 patch overlaps a patch of active Rac1, as detected by the CRIB domain (Figure 6C) (Manser et al., 1994).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging in Figure 6C and supported by citation to Manser et al., 1994.

claim: Rac1 is an upstream regulator of SCAR.
source: Rac1 is an upstream regulator of SCAR, and has been implicated in macropinocytosis (Dumontier et al., 2000; Palmieri et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dumontier et al., 2000 and Palmieri et al., 2000.

claim: Rac1 has been implicated in macropinocytosis.
source: Rac1 is an upstream regulator of SCAR, and has been implicated in macropinocytosis (Dumontier et al., 2000; Palmieri et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dumontier et al., 2000 and Palmieri et al., 2000.

claim: The broad distribution of Rac1 cannot simply account for the much narrower SCAR ring.
source: However, its broad distribution cannot simply account for the much narrower SCAR ring.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the distributions of Rac1 and SCAR in the imaging data.

claim: It has been proposed that PIP3 patch formation requires a positive feedback loop where PIP3 activates Ras.
source: It has been proposed that PIP3 patch formation requires a positive feedback loop where PIP3 activates Ras (Sasaki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sasaki et al., 2007.

claim: A mutant without Ras-activated PI3-kinases and producing only 10% of wild-type PIP3 levels still forms patches of activated Ras at a similar frequency to parental cells.
source: We tested this by genetically manipulating PIP3 levels (Clark et al., 2014; Hoeller and Kay, 2007). A mutant without Ras-activated PI3-kinases and producing only 10% of wild-type PIP3 levels still forms patches of activated Ras at a similar frequency to parental cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of PI3K-null cells in Figure 6D.

claim: Ras patches on the basal surface of PI3-kinase null cells still exclude SCAR from their centre and recruit a peripheral ring of SCAR as normal, albeit more weakly than in parental cells.
source: The SCAR signal in confocal cross sections of macropinocytic cups is too small for an accurate comparison of SCAR ring formation between mutants and therefore we used basal waves as a proxy for macropinocytic cups. Ras patches on the basal surface of PI3-kinase null cells still exclude SCAR from their centre and recruit a peripheral ring of SCAR as normal, albeit more weakly than in parental cells (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy and quantification in Figure 6E-F.

claim: When PIP3 levels are increased 10-fold by eliminating the PTEN phosphatase, the activated Ras domains do not expand correspondingly.
source: Conversely, when PIP3 levels are increased 10-fold by eliminating the PTEN phosphatase, the activated Ras domains do not expand correspondingly (Figure 6G) and remain associated with rings of SCAR (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of PTEN-null cells in Figure 6G.

claim: In PTEN-null cells, activated Ras domains remain associated with rings of SCAR.
source: Conversely, when PIP3 levels are increased 10-fold by eliminating the PTEN phosphatase, the activated Ras domains do not expand correspondingly (Figure 6G) and remain associated with rings of SCAR (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging in Figure 6H.

claim: Ras, rather than PIP3, is the primary determinant of patches and SCAR rings.
source: Thus Ras, rather than PIP3, is the primary determinant of patches and SCAR rings.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic manipulation experiments showing that Ras patches form independently of PIP3 levels.

claim: Latrunculin-A at 1 µM leaves some actin polymerisation intact.
source: We tested this by controlled use of the actin inhibitor latrunculin-A to inhibit ruffle formation. Latrunculin-A at 1 µM leaves some actin polymerisation intact, and at 5 µM abolishes all visible actin filaments, resulting in spherical cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by F-actin imaging in Figure 7A.

claim: Latrunculin-A at 5 µM abolishes all visible actin filaments, resulting in spherical cells.
source: We tested this by controlled use of the actin inhibitor latrunculin-A to inhibit ruffle formation. Latrunculin-A at 1 µM leaves some actin polymerisation intact, and at 5 µM abolishes all visible actin filaments, resulting in spherical cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by F-actin imaging in Figure 7A.

claim: Neither 1 µM nor 5 µM latrunculin-A treatment abolishes the patches of PIP3.
source: Neither treatment abolishes the patches of PIP3, which become larger but less numerous, with a fluorescence intensity not significantly different from control cells (Figure 7B–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PIP3 imaging and quantification in Figure 7B-E.

claim: Latrunculin-A treatment causes PIP3 patches to become larger but less numerous.
source: Neither treatment abolishes the patches of PIP3, which become larger but less numerous, with a fluorescence intensity not significantly different from control cells (Figure 7B–E).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 7C-E.

claim: Latrunculin-A treatment does not significantly change PIP3 patch fluorescence intensity.
source: Neither treatment abolishes the patches of PIP3, which become larger but less numerous, with a fluorescence intensity not significantly different from control cells (Figure 7B–E).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 7C.

claim: Latrunculin-A has little effect on the sharpness of the PIP3 patch boundary.
source: We tested whether the sharp boundaries of patches are affected by latrunculin-A by measuring the intensity across the edges of more than 30 patches for each condition, (Figure 7F–H). It is clear that latrunculin-A has little effect on the sharpness of the patch, suggesting that a diffusion barrier is not required to maintain its strong spatial coherence.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the edge profile analysis in Figure 7F-H.

claim: A diffusion barrier is not required to maintain the strong spatial coherence of PIP3 patches.
source: We tested whether the sharp boundaries of patches are affected by latrunculin-A by measuring the intensity across the edges of more than 30 patches for each condition, (Figure 7F–H). It is clear that latrunculin-A has little effect on the sharpness of the patch, suggesting that a diffusion barrier is not required to maintain its strong spatial coherence.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that patch boundaries remain sharp even when actin is depolymerized.

claim: A circular ruffle is not essential to create signalling patches.
source: In summary, a circular ruffle is not essential to create signalling patches, which appear to largely depend on Ras, with PIP3 playing a secondary though still important role.
evidence: This is concluded from the latrunculin-A experiments showing patches persist without ruffles.

claim: Signalling patches appear to largely depend on Ras, with PIP3 playing a secondary though still important role.
source: In summary, a circular ruffle is not essential to create signalling patches, which appear to largely depend on Ras, with PIP3 playing a secondary though still important role.
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic manipulation experiments showing Ras patches form independently of PIP3 levels.

claim: Macropinocytic cups in NC4 maintain exactly the same organization as in Ax2, with a central patch of PIP3 surround by a ring of SCAR.
source: We found that macropinocytic cups in NC4 maintain exactly the same organization as in Ax2, with a central patch of PIP3 surround by a ring of SCAR, but are much smaller and shorter-lived and often arise de novo (Figure 7I,J and Videos 12, 13 and 14).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of NC4 cells in Figure 7I-J and Videos 12-14.

claim: Macropinocytic cups in NC4 are much smaller and shorter-lived than in Ax2 and often arise de novo.
source: We found that macropinocytic cups in NC4 maintain exactly the same organization as in Ax2, with a central patch of PIP3 surround by a ring of SCAR, but are much smaller and shorter-lived and often arise de novo (Figure 7I,J and Videos 12, 13 and 14).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of NC4 cells in Figure 7I-J and Videos 12-14.

claim: axeB-null cells that have lost NF1 make significantly larger macropinocytic patches compared to cells from the parental strain (p<0.01).
source: To confirm that macropinocytic cup size is controlled by NF1 we compared an isogenic NF1 knock-out with its parent (DdB; also derived from NC4; [Bloomfield et al., 2008]). Cells from each strain were cultivated for 48 hr in axenic medium to maximally induce the rate of macropinocytosis. Under these conditions the axeB-null cells that have lost NF1 make significantly larger macropinocytic patches compared to cells from the parental strain (p<0.01, Figure 7K–L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative comparison in Figure 7K-L.

claim: The intensity of Ras signalling governs the size and frequency of SCAR rings in macropinocytic cups and basal waves.
source: Thus the intensity of Ras signalling governs the size and frequency of SCAR rings in macropinocytic cups and basal waves, showing that Ras must play an instructive role.
evidence: This is concluded from the NF1 mutation experiments showing that increased Ras activity leads to larger patches.

claim: Ras must play an instructive role in macropinocytic cup formation.
source: Thus the intensity of Ras signalling governs the size and frequency of SCAR rings in macropinocytic cups and basal waves, showing that Ras must play an instructive role.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that manipulating Ras activity directly affects patch size and frequency.

claim: Basal PIP3 patches are prevalent in axenic laboratory strains, especially during early starvation.
source: The effect of the loss of NF1 on basal PIP3 patches (basal actin waves) is equally striking. Basal PIP3 patches are prevalent in axenic laboratory strains, especially during early starvation, but absent from all wild-type strains tested (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and compare Videos 15 and 16).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Videos 15-16.

claim: Basal PIP3 patches are absent from all wild-type strains tested.
source: The effect of the loss of NF1 on basal PIP3 patches (basal actin waves) is equally striking. Basal PIP3 patches are prevalent in axenic laboratory strains, especially during early starvation, but absent from all wild-type strains tested (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and compare Videos 15 and 16).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Videos 15-16.

claim: axeB knockout cells that have lost NF1 form abundant basal PIP3 patches, but their wild-type parent does not.
source: axeB knockout cells that have lost NF1 form abundant basal PIP3 patches, but their wild-type parent does not (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Ras patches, assisted by PI3-kinase and Rac, cause macropinocytic cup formation by recruiting rings of SCAR/WAVE complex to their edge.
source: We therefore propose that Ras patches, assisted by PI3-kinase and Rac, cause macropinocytic cup formation by recruiting rings of SCAR/WAVE complex to their edge.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis proposed based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: Cup-shaped plasma membrane structures form from self-organizing patches of active Ras/PIP3, which recruit a ring of actin nucleators to their periphery.
source: We propose that cup-shaped plasma membrane structures form from self-organizing patches of active Ras/PIP3, which recruit a ring of actin nucleators to their periphery.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis stated in the abstract based on all the experimental findings.

claim: Patches are self-organising structures, which can form independently of input from G-protein coupled receptors.
source: PIP3 patches are coincident with patches of activated Ras, which presumably support them by activating PI3-kinase, and also of activated Rac. Previous work suggest that patches are self-organising structures, which can form independently of input from G-protein coupled receptors (Sasaki et al., 2007) and are likely dependent on positive feedback loops between their components (Postma et al., 2003, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sasaki et al., 2007.

claim: Patches are likely dependent on positive feedback loops between their components.
source: PIP3 patches are coincident with patches of activated Ras, which presumably support them by activating PI3-kinase, and also of activated Rac. Previous work suggest that patches are self-organising structures, which can form independently of input from G-protein coupled receptors (Sasaki et al., 2007) and are likely dependent on positive feedback loops between their components (Postma et al., 2003, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Postma et al., 2003, 2004.

claim: The kinetics that lead to patch formation must lie largely within the compass of the GEFs and GAPs activating and inactivating Ras.
source: Our results argue against an essential role for feedback from PIP3 to Ras, because activated Ras patches can form independently of type-1 PI3-kinases and are still able to recruit SCAR to their edges, albeit less efficiently than when PI3-kinases are present. Thus it appears that the kinetics that lead to patch formation must lie largely within the compass of the GEFs and GAPs activating and inactivating Ras.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Ras patches form independently of PI3-kinases.

claim: Myosin-1 is genetically important for macropinocytosis in Dictyostelium.
source: Alternatively, SCAR might be moved to the periphery of Ras/PIP3 patches, perhaps by myosin-1 motors. Early work showed that myosin-1 is genetically important for macropinocytosis in Dictyostelium (Novak et al., 1995; Titus, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Novak et al., 1995 and Titus, 2000.

claim: Myosin-1 isoforms are recruited to macropinocytic cups in both Dictyostelium and Acanthamoeba.
source: In support of the genetic evidence, myosin-1 isoforms are recruited to macropinocytic cups in both Dictyostelium and Acanthamoeba (Brzeska et al., 2012; Ostap et al., 2003), most likely due to their affinity for PIP3 (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brzeska et al., 2012; Ostap et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2012.

claim: The PIP3-binding MyoE and MyoF are recruited in the centre and MyoB at the periphery of macropinocytic cups, forming a 'bull's eye' pattern.
source: The PIP3-binding MyoE and MyoF are recruited in the centre and MyoB at the periphery of macropinocytic cups, forming a striking 'bull's eye' pattern (Brzeska et al., 2016; Dieckmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brzeska et al., 2016 and Dieckmann et al., 2010.

claim: The basal actin waves appear to be formed as a consequence of the loss of NF1 in standard laboratory axenic strains.
source: First, the basal actin waves, which give a valuable window into actin dynamics (Bretschneider et al., 2004, 2009; Gerisch, 2010), appear to be formed as a consequence of the loss of NF1 in standard laboratory axenic strains.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that basal waves are present in axenic strains but absent in wild-type strains with functional NF1.

claim: All patches of PIP3 and activated Ras are related by their common recruitment of SCAR to their periphery.
source: Second, we consider that all patches of PIP3 and activated Ras are related by their common recruitment of SCAR to their periphery and are therefore likely to organise circular rings of actin polymerization, rather than the solid blocks characteristic of pseudopods.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that SCAR rings are found at all PIP3 patches examined.

claim: PIP3 patches are likely to organise circular rings of actin polymerization, rather than the solid blocks characteristic of pseudopods.
source: Second, we consider that all patches of PIP3 and activated Ras are related by their common recruitment of SCAR to their periphery and are therefore likely to organise circular rings of actin polymerization, rather than the solid blocks characteristic of pseudopods.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SCAR forms rings around PIP3 patches, not solid blocks.

claim: The proposed role of PIP3 patches in chemotaxis needs to be re-evaluated.
source: Therefore, the proposed role of these patches in chemotaxis, where they have been mistaken for pseudopods, needs to be re-evaluated.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that PIP3 patches organize circular actin structures, not pseudopods.
